lines.text: Grassland kingdoms, three colonial powers, two official languages and a team that lit up a World Cup. This is the story of Cameroon.
Late in the fourteenth century the Bamum kingdom rose in the western highlands, one of several kingdoms of the grasslands.
Its king Ibrahim Njoya did something rare: he invented a whole script so his people could write their own language.
In 1884 Germany claimed the land as the colony of Kamerun. During the First World War, France and Britain took it and split it between them.
In the late 1880s the Germans founded a post at Yaounde, the city that would become the capital.
Ruben Um Nyobe led the fight for independence, and was killed in 1958 before he could see it.
Ahmadou Ahidjo would become the first president of the new country.
The novelist Mongo Beti wrote against colonial rule, and later against the rulers who followed it.
Paul Biya, born in 1933, would take power in 1982, and remain president for more than four decades.
Born that same year, the saxophonist Manu Dibango would carry Cameroon's sound to the world with Soul Makossa.
Roger Milla would become a legend at the 1990 World Cup, dancing by the corner flag after his goals.
In 1960 Cameroon became independent, and later joined its French and British parts into one country.
Samuel Eto'o would grow up to win the Champions League three times, one of Africa's finest strikers.
In 1986 a cloud of gas burst from Lake Nyos and silently killed some seventeen hundred people.
Francis Ngannou, born that same year, would rise from poverty to become heavyweight champion of mixed martial arts.
From Nigeria, the Boko Haram insurgency spread into Cameroon's Far North, bringing years of violence.
And since 2017 the English-speaking regions have been torn by conflict, over the country's divided past.
Shaped by many rulers and two languages, Cameroon is still working out how to be one nation.
